overview: The Khitan-led Liao was a major northern Asian empire, joining grassland, farming and urban communities and negotiating with Song China as a powerful rival. This map record spans 900-1200, but its coarse northeastern outlines begin before Abaoji's rise and continue after the dynasty's conquest in 1125. They are snapshots, not precise annual frontiers. The western successor known as Qara Khitai had a separate Central Asian history.

periods.title: Abaoji rises
periods.summary: Abaoji became Khitan khan in 907;916 is commonly used for his proclamation as emperor. These dates mark different steps in a debated foundation.

periods.title: A northern imperial power
periods.summary: The Liao established itself as a major rival of the Chinese states to its south, with power reaching into northern Chinese territory.

periods.title: Peace, patronage and building
periods.summary: The 1005 peace settlement brought regular Song payments; surviving buildings and religious projects reveal Liao patronage.

periods.title: Jurchen advance
periods.summary: Jurchen attacks culminated in the capture of the last Liao emperor in 1125. Some Khitans had already moved west.

sections.title: Rulers, neighbors and the people they governed

items.text: Why do books give both 907 and 916 as the beginning? Abaoji became khan in 907, while 916 commonly marks his declaration as emperor. Historian Pujiang Liu compares conflicting records rather than pretending the choice is simple. An empire could grow through several steps before later historians assigned it one official birthday.

Liao government had northern and southern administrations. The northern branch served pastoral and partly agricultural regions; the southern branch handled densely settled farming and town districts. Duties included taxes, legal cases and military horses. Officials' ancestry did not divide neatly into two separate teams: some powerful families served in both branches.

Empresses and empress dowagers could be formidable political figures. Hang Lin's study of Yingtian and Chengtian describes women directing government and military affairs; some consorts shared authority while their husbands were still alive. Skill with horses and weapons mattered at this court. These were powerful elite women, rather than evidence that every woman enjoyed the same freedoms.

The peace of 1005 required Song to send Liao 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk annually. A tael was a weight measure, not one standard coin. A Song silver ingot found in Linxi County may have been part of such payments, according to the museum caption reproduced by Columbia. Diplomacy could arrive as a very heavy delivery.

On wooden coffin panels from the tenth or early eleventh century, servants prepare an outdoor banquet. Two carry a table already covered with drinking vessels; others haul containers, probably of wine. The deceased was imagined as the honored guest. These are carefully composed wishes for the afterlife, but they preserve wonderfully practical details of organizing a feast.

Another panel shows women carrying offerings: one wears a flowing Chinese-style gown, while others have Khitan hairstyles and dress. Shorter clothing and tall boots suited riding. Elsewhere, seated boys have two attentive dogs beside them. A thousand years later, those dogs still look ready to notice anything interesting happening near dinner.

A ceramic flask in Michigan preserves the shape of a leather bag used by horse riders. Its flattened body has holes for a carrying strap and a short spout at one side. The museum connects such leather containers with kumis, fermented mare's milk. Potters translated a familiar portable container into glazed clay, including the details that made its model recognizable.

Splendid tombs and court clothes depended on other people's labor. Crossley describes dependent workers on aristocratic estates raising crops and animals or producing pottery, cloth and weapons. Rank and freedom varied sharply. Looking at a beautiful object also invites a practical question: who grew its raw materials, made it, and controlled the maker's work?

sections.title: Builders, books and a surviving written voice

items.text: The wooden pagoda at Yingxian was completed in 1056. About 67 meters high, it uses an octagonal plan, an inner and outer structural frame, and sophisticated timber joinery. Its survival makes it a remarkable place to study Liao carpentry. The nearby region's monumental buildings required skilled planning, not simply a very tall pile of wood.

A life-size glazed ceramic luohan, a Buddhist holy figure, now stands in the Metropolitan Museum. Its careful modeling and three-color glaze reveal ambitious ceramic workshops around 1000. Material found at an ancient kiln near Beijing in 1983 helped establish the group's late-tenth- or eleventh-century date. The often-repeated story that the figures came from a particular cave remains less secure.

At Cloud Dwelling Monastery, monks engraved 4,080 stone slabs between 1093 and 1095, then buried them in 1117 to protect Buddhist scriptures. This continued a project begun centuries earlier. It was an extraordinarily heavy backup library: preserving a book meant organizing stone, copying and carving, rather than simply putting another paper copy on a shelf.

Liao scholars also produced a Buddhist canon printed from wooden blocks, completed in 1068. The stone-carving project used versions from this printed collection. Books and inscriptions therefore worked together: a text could move from a printing workshop to a stone surface intended to last much longer.

A 1118 pillar at the monastery contains the Chinese words “雲居寺”, meaning “Cloud Dwelling Monastery”. They appear in its title, preserved in a rubbing. This is an actual Liao-period written sample in Chinese; it is not Khitan script. The inscription records the labor of preserving Buddhist texts.

Education could cross cultural boundaries. Yelü Dashi, later leader of the western successor state, received both Khitan and Chinese education. He was also an accomplished mounted warrior. For an aristocrat like him, book learning and practical military skills belonged to the same career.

The Khitan name traveled far beyond the dynasty's borders. Forms such as Cathay became European names for China, while related forms spread across Eurasia. It is a striking legacy: people could use a name derived from the Khitans long after Liao emperors had disappeared from the political map.

ending.text: The Jurchens captured the last Liao emperor in 1125, ending the dynasty in its eastern homeland. Some Khitans moved west with Yelü Dashi and established the Qara Khitai successor empire in Central Asia. The imported 1200 cutoff does not mark Liao's actual fall or the disappearance of Khitan communities.
